newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Labor still sliding after eight months.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Labor still sliding after eight months.

text.p: The Labor Opposition is in deeper trouble than most people realise.
It is only now dawning on the consciousness of the political scene that there is something deeply, deeply wrong with the Labor Party and Opposition Leader Kim Beazley.
The evidence is the opinion polls, the only objective data we ever get about politics between one election and the next.
Almost every political factor one can think of suggests that Labor should have mounted a comeback since the election, or certainly since the government's honeymoon peaked in May.
Instead it is still sliding, as the Reuters Poll Trend shows. (See separate report for full data.)
The government won the election with primary vote lead of 8.5 percent.
It was the biggest landslide in 20 years and, as readers familiar with financial market movements would appreciate, it might well have been followed by a correction, or at least a muted honeymoon.
Instead the honeymoon took the government to a lead of about 18 percentage points, more than double its commanding election lead.

That faded, as one might have expected, but the astounding development has been that since the budget the government's standing has started strengthening again. The primary-vote lead is now 15 points.
But most disturbing for Labor is Kim Beazley's standing.
It was only to be expected that Beazley would start well behind Prime Minister John Howard as preferred leader.
Even so, it was a shock to see Beazley in May fully 38 points behind Howard, who has himself never inspired the country.
But it was confidently predicted then, and with good reason, that Beazley's profile gradually would rise, lifting his voter support with it.
And his standing did rise, for a while, but is now almost incredibly fading again. He is becoming less popular as the country gets to know him more as opposition leader.
This is critical for Labor. The party has no hope electorally while its leader is so far behind and falling even further behind.
Yet all this has happened against the background of the new government slashing programmes in the budget and pressing ahead with unpopular micro-economic reforms such as the Telstra privatisation.
The government has suffered severe embarrassment over ministerial conflict of interest and unemployment is rising.
Labor's frontbench continues to glitter with talent, as it did in government, while many of the Liberal-National ministers fail to impress.
But for Labor the polls are shifting from disasterous to hideous.
The Lindsey by-election was not a flash in the pan. It showed the true electoral standing of the opposition.
On final point.
Of course no election is about to be held now, but if one were, the polls suggest the already shellshocked Labor Party would lose about half of its remaining seats in the House of Representatives.
Only the safest working class seats would remain.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
